home-remodeling.h1: Miami Beach Homes, Rebuilt From the Studs
home-remodeling.hero_sub: Whole-home remodels for Miami Beach houses and condos: gut renovations, structural openings, new systems, impact glazing. Licensed and insured (CGC1539072), every project permitted, inspected, and supervised on site daily.
intro_paragraphs: Miami Beach housing stock covers a full century of ambition: 1920s Mediterranean Revival off Pine Tree Drive, 1930s Art Deco in Flamingo Park, postwar MiMo blocks in Mid-Beach and North Beach, and glass-walled contemporary estates on North Bay Road, the Sunset Islands, and Palm and Hibiscus Islands. What most of these homes share is a plan drawn for another era. The whole-home remodels we run here open layouts, replace every aging system behind the walls, add impact glazing, and keep the architecture that made the street worth buying on in the first place.

Permitting belongs to the City of Miami Beach Building Department, and that is rarely the whole story. In local historic districts like Flamingo Park and Altos del Mar, exterior changes need a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Historic Preservation Board; outside them, projects seeking waivers or variances go to the Design Review Board. Every window and door must carry High-Velocity Hurricane Zone product approvals, and on a barrier island the FEMA substantial-improvement rule can decide whether a gut renovation also becomes an elevation conversation. We plan the approval path before demolition, not after a correction notice.

Behind PGX Builders Group sit more than two decades of South Florida building and 150-plus remodels and additions, all permitted, all inspected — experience a barrier island rewards. On Miami Beach that experience looks like a fixed written scope before the first wall opens, a supervisor on site daily, floors and finishes protected while trades move through, and crews who understand that a guard gate on Star Island is not a suggestion. One licensed team, Lic. CGC1539072, carries your remodel from estimate to warranty, so there is exactly one phone number to call and it answers.

home-remodeling.scope_intro: Every whole-home remodel is scoped in writing before work begins. Here is what that scope typically covers on a Miami Beach project.

scope_items.name: Full-gut renovations
scope_items.desc: Down to block and back: new layouts, plumbing, electrical, mechanical, insulation, and finishes, sequenced so inspections pass the first time.

scope_items.desc: Miami-Dade approved glazing throughout, sized to historic openings where boards require it, installed with flashing details a salt-air address demands.

scope_items.desc: Stucco, eyebrows, curved corners, and original Deco detail restored carefully while everything behind them quietly becomes a modern house.

scope_items.name: Complete MEP replacement

faqs.q: Do I need Historic Preservation Board approval to remodel in Miami Beach?
faqs.a: Only if your property sits in a designated historic district and the work changes the exterior. Interior remodels generally need building permits but not board review. In districts like Flamingo Park or Altos del Mar, exterior alterations require a Certificate of Appropriateness; many are approved at staff level, while larger changes go to a public hearing. We check your property's status before design starts and prepare the submittal so the answer arrives before demolition day.

faqs.q: How long do remodeling permits take in Miami Beach?
faqs.a: It depends on scope. Straightforward interior remodels move fastest; projects needing Historic Preservation Board or Design Review Board hearings follow monthly board calendars, which can add months to the front end. We do not quote fantasy timelines. We map the actual approval path for your property, submit complete drawings the first time, and track the review so your project is not the one sitting in a queue with unanswered comments.

faqs.q: What is the FEMA 50 percent rule and will it affect my project?
faqs.a: If the cost of improvements exceeds half of your building's market value, federal flood rules treat the project as a substantial improvement, and the entire structure must be brought into compliance with current flood elevation requirements. On a barrier island like Miami Beach, that can reshape a remodel's scope or phasing. We run this math with you early, in writing, so the rule informs the design instead of ambushing the budget.

faqs.q: How much does a whole-home remodel cost in Miami Beach?
faqs.a: Wide honest answer: it depends on square footage, structural changes, and the level of finish, and Miami Beach carries real premiums for historic detail, flood compliance, and island logistics. We are a high-end contractor, not the low bid, and we would rather give you an accurate number after a walk-through than a pleasant one over the phone. Every PGX project starts with a fixed written scope, so the price you approve is the price we manage to.

faqs.q: Can you remodel a condo unit as well as a house?
faqs.a: Yes. Miami Beach condo remodels are their own discipline: association plan approval, certificates of insurance, service-elevator reservations, floor protection in common corridors, and strict working hours. Since Florida's milestone inspection requirements arrived, boards have become more careful about licensed, insured contractors — which works in your favor, because that is the only way we operate. We manage the building relationship so you do not spend your renovation refereeing between the contractor and the property manager.

kitchen-remodeling.title: Custom Kitchen Remodeling, Miami Beach FL | PGX Builders
kitchen-remodeling.meta_description: Custom kitchen remodeling in Miami Beach: cabinetry, stone and layout changes for island estates and condo towers alike. Schedule a walk-through: (786) 273-2524.
kitchen-remodeling.h1: Kitchens Built for Miami Beach Living
kitchen-remodeling.hero_sub: Custom kitchens for Miami Beach homes and condo towers: cabinetry built to order, stone templated on site, layouts opened up legally — permitted, inspected, and managed by one licensed team every day.
kitchen-remodeling.local_heading: From Flamingo Park Galleys to Island Estates
intro_paragraphs: A Miami Beach kitchen has range in every sense. In Flamingo Park and the Deco streets of South Beach, owners are unwinding narrow 1930s galleys into rooms people actually gather in. On North Bay Road and the Sunset Islands, kitchens run to catering scale — double islands, wine walls, prep pantries — because the house hosts forty as often as four. And in the towers of South of Fifth, a full kitchen rebuild happens inside a condo's rules. We design and build for all three, with custom cabinetry and stone work as the constant.

Even an interior-only kitchen runs through the City of Miami Beach Building Department, because moving gas, relocating appliances, or touching a drain line means permits and trade inspections. In a condo, add the association layer: board approval of plans, insurance certificates, elevator reservations, and workday noise windows. In the post-milestone-inspection era, boards read renovation paperwork more carefully than ever. In historic-district houses, a new window over the sink brings the Historic Preservation Board into your kitchen. We have processed enough of these approvals to keep them boring.

What makes a PGX kitchen different is the discipline around it. The scope is fixed in writing — cabinetry line, stone slabs, appliance schedule, lighting plan — before we open a wall, so the budget does not drift with the tide. A site supervisor is there every day, protecting floors that are staying and neighbors who are not moving. Cabinetry is measured after the walls are true, not before, and stone is templated on site. For twenty-plus years and over 150 projects across South Florida, that sequence is why our kitchens finish level, plumb, and on speaking terms with their owners.
kitchen-remodeling.scope_heading: What We Build Into Miami Beach Kitchens
kitchen-remodeling.scope_intro: From Deco-cottage galleys to double-island estate kitchens, these are the five things we get asked to build most often on the Beach.

scope_items.name: Custom cabinetry
scope_items.desc: Built-to-order boxes and fronts in humidity-stable finishes, fitted to walls that are rarely square in a 1935 house, with hardware that shrugs off salt air.

scope_items.name: Stone counters and islands
scope_items.desc: Marble, quartzite, and porcelain slabs templated on site, with islands engineered for seating, storage, and the occasional buffet for fifty.

scope_items.name: Layout and wall changes
scope_items.desc: Opening galley kitchens to dining rooms and terrace views with engineered headers and proper permits, so the cook stops working in a hallway.

scope_items.name: Appliance and gas relocation
scope_items.desc: Rerouting gas, water, and ventilation for new appliance walls, permitted and inspected, and planned around riser realities when the kitchen lives in a tower.

scope_items.name: Lighting design
scope_items.desc: Task light where you prep, ambient light where you gather, accents on the stone — every layer dimmable, because good marble deserves good light.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to remodel my kitchen in Miami Beach?
faqs.a: If the project moves plumbing, gas, electrical, or walls — and a real kitchen remodel almost always does — yes, through the City of Miami Beach Building Department, with trade inspections along the way. Purely cosmetic swaps like counters or cabinet fronts on existing footprints may not require one. We permit everything that needs it, because unpermitted kitchen work has a way of surfacing at appraisal or closing, at the least convenient possible moment.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a kitchen in a South of Fifth or Collins Avenue condo?
faqs.a: Yes, condo kitchens are a regular part of our Miami Beach work. Expect association review of your plans, proof of licensing and insurance, elevator scheduling, and defined work hours; some buildings also restrict wet-over-dry layout changes, which limits where sinks and appliances can move. We read your building's alteration agreement before we design, so the kitchen you fall in love with is one your board will actually approve.

faqs.q: How long does a custom kitchen remodel take?
faqs.a: The honest driver is cabinetry lead time, which for true custom work is measured in months, not weeks, so we run design, permitting, and ordering in parallel. Site construction on a typical high-end kitchen spans several weeks to a few months depending on structural changes. What we do not do is demolish your kitchen and then start waiting on cabinets. Demolition begins when the long-lead items are real.

faqs.q: What does a high-end kitchen cost in Miami Beach?
faqs.a: Custom cabinetry, natural stone, and appliance packages set the range more than square footage does, and it is a wide range. We position ourselves at the craftsmanship end of the market, so our numbers reflect real custom work, licensed trades, and full permitting rather than a resurfacing job with new handles. After one walk-through we will give you a written scope with a fixed price — a more useful document than any ballpark.

faqs.q: Does salt air really affect kitchen materials this close to the ocean?
faqs.a: It does, and oceanside blocks feel it most. Standard steel hardware pits, budget appliance finishes corrode, and unsealed natural stone absorbs more than it should in constant humidity. We specify marine-grade stainless, quality plated or solid-brass hardware, and sealed or porcelain surfaces where exposure is high, especially in homes that open to terraces and let the outside in. The upgrade cost is modest; replacing corroded finishes in five years is not.

kitchen-remodeling.cta_sub: Bring your inspiration photos and your building's rules if you have them. We will handle the rest — walk-throughs and estimates in English o en español.

bathroom-remodeling.title: Miami Beach Bathroom Remodeling Done Right | PGX Builders
bathroom-remodeling.meta_description: Bathroom remodeling in Miami Beach FL: primary suites, frameless showers and waterproofing built for barrier-island humidity. Estimates at (786) 273-2524.
bathroom-remodeling.hero_sub: Primary suites, frameless showers, and stone baths built for barrier-island humidity — full waterproofing systems, city permits and inspections handled, and daily supervision from one licensed, insured team.
bathroom-remodeling.local_heading: Waterproofing for an Island That Tests It
intro_paragraphs: The primary bath is where Miami Beach homes show their age first. Original 1930s houses in Flamingo Park and Palm View hide small mosaic-tiled bathrooms that were charming for about sixty years; Mid-Beach ranches and MiMo-era homes carry 1980s remodels of 1950s plumbing; and even newer island estates on La Gorce and Allison Island reach the point where travertine and brass bought in 2004 has to go. Owners here rebuild toward the same brief: a real primary suite, a frameless shower you can live in, stone that reads calm, and a freestanding tub with a view if the lot allows.

Bathroom permits in Miami Beach are straightforward on paper — City of Miami Beach Building Department, plumbing and electrical inspections, tile after the shower pan passes — and unforgiving in practice. In condominium buildings from South of Fifth to Collins Avenue, wet-area renovations also need association sign-off, protection of the unit below, and respect for plumbing risers that serve forty neighbors. Florida's milestone-inspection era has made boards notably more attentive to who is opening walls and whether they are licensed. We are, visibly: Lic. CGC1539072 on every permit card.

Waterproofing is where we are least flexible, because a barrier island gives water too many ways in: from above, from below, and from the air itself. Every PGX bathroom gets a full waterproofing membrane system, flood-tested pans, sealed niches, and ventilation sized for actual Miami Beach humidity rather than a code minimum. The scope is written and fixed before demolition, one supervisor checks the work daily, and finishes elsewhere in the home stay under protection until we hand back the keys. It is the detail nobody sees and, on our projects, nobody regrets.
bathroom-remodeling.scope_intro: Whether it is a 1936 house or a bay-view tower, a PGX bathroom includes these elements — each permitted, inspected, and waterproofed like it matters.

scope_items.name: Primary suite conversions
scope_items.desc: Borrowing a closet or spare room to create a true suite: double vanity, water closet, walk-in shower, and storage that finally fits.

scope_items.name: Frameless and curbless showers
scope_items.desc: Curbless where the slab allows, full membrane waterproofing, flood-tested pans, linear drains, and heavy glass set to survive daily use and holiday guests.

scope_items.name: Freestanding tubs and stone
scope_items.desc: Sculptural tubs, book-matched slabs, and large-format porcelain, installed over substrates prepared for South Florida moisture and movement.

scope_items.name: Condo bathroom rebuilds
scope_items.desc: Wet-area renovations in Miami Beach towers, run to association rules: approved plans, protected corridors, scheduled elevators, and quiet hours honored.

scope_items.name: Ventilation and moisture control
scope_items.desc: Properly ducted exhaust, dehumidification where warranted, and details that keep a tightly sealed impact-glass house from growing things it should not.

faqs.q: Is a permit needed to redo a bathroom in Miami Beach?
faqs.a: Any remodel that touches plumbing, electrical, or waterproofed assemblies does — which describes essentially every real bathroom renovation. The City of Miami Beach Building Department inspects rough plumbing, electrical, and the shower pan before tile goes on, which is exactly the sequence you want: those inspections protect you from failures that only show up after the marble is grouted. Cosmetic-only updates on existing fixtures may skip permitting, but that is rarely the project people call us for.

faqs.q: Can you remodel a bathroom in an older Miami Beach condo tower?
faqs.a: Yes, and the building's age shapes the plan. Older towers have original plumbing risers and strict rules about moving wet areas, and since Florida's milestone inspection law took effect, associations scrutinize renovation applications more closely. We prepare the full package — plans, license, insurance certificates, contractor rules acknowledgment — and schedule tie-ins to building plumbing at hours the association allows. Your neighbors two floors down should learn about your renovation from you, not from their ceiling.

faqs.q: How do you keep a new bathroom from growing mold here?
faqs.a: Three layers: waterproofing, ventilation, and materials. We install full membrane systems behind tile, not just cement board, flood-test shower pans before finishing, and duct exhaust fans to the exterior with enough capacity for a steam-heavy household. In tightly sealed homes with impact glass, we size ventilation deliberately, because modern envelopes trap humidity better than the 1940s ever did. Materials that do not feed mold, plus air that actually leaves the room, is the whole formula.

faqs.q: How long does a primary bathroom renovation take?
faqs.a: Once materials are on hand and permits issued, a full gut of a primary bath typically runs a number of weeks on site: demolition, rough trades, inspections, waterproofing, tile, stone, glass, fixtures, punch list. The variables that stretch it are structural surprises in older houses and long-lead items like custom vanities and specialty stone. We schedule around reality — nothing gets demolished until the critical materials are confirmed, so your house is not down a bathroom while a slab sits in a quarry.

faqs.q: Is it worth using natural stone in a beach-climate bathroom?
faqs.a: Yes, with eyes open. Marble and quartzite are beautiful and perfectly viable here when sealed properly, set on waterproofed substrates, and maintained; porcelain slabs that convincingly mimic stone are the lower-maintenance alternative for steam showers and heavy-use baths. We walk clients through both honestly, including which stones etch, which shrug it off, and where each belongs. The wrong answer is choosing a delicate stone and pretending the humidity will make an exception for you.

home-additions.title: Home Additions & Second Stories, Miami Beach FL | PGX Builders
home-additions.meta_description: Home additions in Miami Beach: rear extensions and second stories designed around freeboard and the FEMA 50 percent rule. Talk to PGX at (786) 273-2524.
home-additions.h1: More House, Above the Flood Line
home-additions.hero_sub: Rear extensions, second stories, and guest suites across Miami Beach — engineered, permitted through the city, and built to current flood and hurricane code by a licensed contractor who supervises daily.
home-additions.local_heading: Growing a House on a Regulated Island
intro_paragraphs: Lots in Miami Beach are finite in a way that concentrates the mind, so when a family outgrows a house on Pine Tree Drive or a Sunset Islands lot, the answer is usually up or back rather than out of the neighborhood. We build rear extensions that open 1930s and 1950s homes toward pool and bay, second-story additions over strengthened first floors, garage conversions, and guest suites for the in-laws who visit every winter and stay longer each year. Done well, an addition reads like the house always intended it — that is the standard we permit and build to.

If Miami Beach regulation has a reputation, additions are why. The City of Miami Beach Building Department reviews structure, zoning checks lot coverage and setbacks, and the FEMA substantial-improvement rule sits over everything: if your project's value crosses the fifty percent threshold, the whole house must meet current flood elevation standards, including the city's freeboard requirement above base flood elevation. In historic districts, the Historic Preservation Board expects additions to stand politely behind the original facade. None of this is a reason not to build; it is a reason to design with the rules in the room from day one.

Structure is the quiet half of every addition here. Second stories on pre-war masonry mean tie-beam upgrades, new columns, and foundations verified before anyone talks about finishes; PGX brings the engineers in early and prices that work into a fixed written scope instead of discovering it at month three. Our 20-plus years in South Florida and 150-plus delivered projects taught us to sequence additions so the family keeps living in the house while it grows. Daily supervision, protected interiors, and one accountable license from first sketch to final inspection — that is the whole pitch.
home-additions.scope_heading: How We Build Additions on the Beach
home-additions.scope_intro: Additions here are equal parts architecture, engineering, and paperwork. This is the work we plan, permit, and build.

scope_items.name: Rear extensions
scope_items.desc: New family rooms and primary suites extending toward pool and water, tied into the existing structure with engineered footings and connections.

scope_items.name: Second-story additions
scope_items.desc: Full upper floors over reinforced first stories, with engineering, tie beams, and stairs placed where the plan wants them rather than where they merely fit.

scope_items.name: Garage and loggia conversions
scope_items.desc: Turning underused garages and loggias into offices, gyms, or guest quarters, with the insulation and cooling that make them genuinely livable in high summer.

scope_items.name: In-law and guest suites
scope_items.desc: Self-contained suites with baths and kitchenettes where zoning allows, designed for long visits that stay pleasant on both sides of the guest room door.

scope_items.name: Tie beams and foundations
scope_items.desc: Structural upgrades that let older Miami Beach masonry carry new loads, verified by engineers, inspected by the city, and hidden by the finish work.

faqs.q: Will an addition trigger the FEMA 50 percent rule on my house?
faqs.a: It can. If the value of the work exceeds fifty percent of the building's market value, the entire home must be brought up to current flood standards, including elevation requirements — a very different project than the addition you sketched. Miami Beach applies these rules carefully, and so do we: before design goes far, we help you understand where your project stands relative to the threshold and what the options are on either side of it.

faqs.q: Can my 1930s Miami Beach house support a second story?
faqs.a: Often yes, after engineering confirms it. Pre-war masonry homes typically need tie-beam upgrades, reinforced columns, and sometimes foundation work before they carry a new floor — all solvable, all priceable, and all better discovered in design than in demolition. If the house is a contributing structure in a historic district, the second story also needs to sit respectfully behind the original massing to earn board approval. We handle the engineers, the drawings, and the hearing.

faqs.q: Do additions in Miami Beach historic districts face extra review?
faqs.a: Yes. In districts like Flamingo Park, additions to contributing homes go through Certificate of Appropriateness review, and the board's consistent preference is clear: keep the addition subordinate to the original house, set it back from the street, and let the historic facade keep telling the story. Working within that framework is a design skill, not a limitation. Some of the best additions on the Beach are invisible from the sidewalk and transformative from the backyard.

faqs.q: How long does a home addition take from design to completion?
faqs.a: Plan in phases: design and engineering first, then permitting — longer if a board hearing is involved — then construction, which for a substantial addition typically runs several months on site. Miami Beach reviews are thorough, and waterfront or historic properties add layers. We give you a milestone schedule at contract, keep the permit moving with complete submittals, and sequence construction so the occupied part of your home stays livable, secure, and air conditioned throughout.

faqs.q: Is it smarter to add on or move?
faqs.a: On this island, often the former. Miami Beach lots in the neighborhoods people actually want — the islands, North Bay Road, the golf-course streets — rarely come up, and transaction costs on high-value homes are their own renovation budget. An addition lets you keep the location and fix the house. We will tell you honestly if your lot, structure, or flood situation argues otherwise; an accurate no early is cheaper than an optimistic yes later.

home-additions.cta_sub: Before you list the house, let us look at the lot. Addition feasibility, flood math, and honest numbers, in English o en español.

outdoor-living.title: Outdoor Living & Exterior Work in Miami Beach | PGX Builders
outdoor-living.meta_description: Outdoor living construction in Miami Beach: terraces, summer kitchens and pergolas built for salt, sun and hurricane code. Schedule a site visit: (786) 273-2524.
outdoor-living.h1: Outdoor Rooms Built for Salt and Sun
outdoor-living.hero_sub: Terraces, summer kitchens, pergolas, and full exterior renovations for Miami Beach homes — HVHZ-rated, permitted, and built from materials that treat salt air as a given, not a surprise. Licensed, insured, supervised every working day.
outdoor-living.local_heading: The Backyard Ends at the Bay
intro_paragraphs: On Miami Beach the backyard often ends in a seawall, which raises the stakes for everything between the kitchen door and the water. Owners on the Sunset Islands, Palm and Hibiscus Islands, and North Bay Road invest in covered terraces, summer kitchens, and pergolas that turn bay frontage into the most used room of the house; inland, Flamingo Park and Bayshore yards trade lawn for shaded dining terraces and rebuilt pool decks. The common thread is exposure — sun from above, salt from every direction — and the materials have to be chosen like they know it.

Exterior work is the most regulated square footage in Miami Beach. The City of Miami Beach Building Department permits terraces, summer kitchens, driveways, and roof work; anything visible from the street in a historic district goes through Certificate of Appropriateness review; and impact doors, shutters, and glazing must carry High-Velocity Hurricane Zone approvals. Drainage matters more here than almost anywhere, because king tides are not hypothetical on a barrier island, and seawall or dock work brings its own county environmental permitting, which we coordinate rather than leave orphaned. Bring us the wish list; we will bring the approval map.

Outdoor projects on the islands come with logistics most contractors underestimate: guard gates with contractor rules, narrow streets where a concrete truck needs a plan, and neighbors close enough to review your work ethic in real time. PGX runs these sites the way we run interiors — fixed written scope, daily supervision, clean staging, crews in and out on schedule. Marine-grade stainless in the summer kitchen, porcelain pavers that stay cool and ignore salt, stucco and paint systems specified for oceanfront exposure. After 20-plus years building in South Florida, we know exactly which shortcuts the climate eventually invoices.
outdoor-living.scope_intro: Outdoor scope on Miami Beach runs from the back door to the seawall. These are the pieces we build most.

scope_items.name: Covered terraces and pergolas
scope_items.desc: Shade structures engineered for hurricane wind loads, detailed to frame the bay view rather than block it, and permitted before the first post is set.

scope_items.name: Summer kitchens
scope_items.desc: Grills, refrigeration, and prep counters in marine-grade stainless and stone, with gas and electrical runs permitted and inspected like the indoor kitchen they rival.

scope_items.name: Pool decks and driveways
scope_items.desc: Porcelain and shellstone surfaces set over real drainage design, so a king-tide week ends with wet streets rather than a flooded terrace.

scope_items.name: Stucco and exterior paint
scope_items.desc: Whole-envelope refreshes with crack repair and coating systems specified for salt exposure, done once and correctly instead of every third year.

scope_items.name: Impact openings and roofing
scope_items.desc: Miami-Dade approved doors, windows, and shutters, plus roofing sequenced alongside exterior work so the trades do not undo each other.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a pergola or summer kitchen in Miami Beach?
faqs.a: Yes on both counts. Pergolas and other shade structures need building permits and must meet High-Velocity Hurricane Zone wind-load requirements; summer kitchens add gas, electrical, and sometimes plumbing permits on top. If the work is visible from the street in a historic district, Certificate of Appropriateness review applies too. It sounds like a lot because it is — which is exactly why our proposals include the permitting, not a footnote wishing you luck with it.

faqs.q: Can you work on the gated islands — Star, Palm, Hibiscus, Sunset?
faqs.a: Yes. Gated and guard-staffed communities have contractor rules: registration at the gate, insurance on file, defined working hours, and expectations about how crews behave on quiet streets. We plan deliveries so a stone truck is not idling at the guardhouse, keep staging tight, and leave the site clean daily. Discretion is part of the service on these streets; our teams finish beautiful work without becoming neighborhood news.

faqs.q: Can you handle seawall or dock work as part of an outdoor project?
faqs.a: Seawalls and docks carry their own environmental permitting through county and state agencies, typically with specialized marine contractors performing the in-water work. What we do is coordinate: designing terraces, decks, and landscape structures so they meet the seawall correctly, sequencing our work around marine construction, and making sure the upland drainage does not fight the waterfront. You get one coherent project instead of two contractors pointing at each other across the property line.

faqs.q: Which outdoor materials actually hold up near the ocean?
faqs.a: Porcelain pavers, properly sealed dense stones, marine-grade stainless, powder-coated aluminum, and true exterior hardwoods or their better composites. What fails: standard steel fasteners, bargain fixture finishes, untreated softwoods, and any coating applied over damp stucco. Salt air is patient and works nights and weekends. We specify for the exposure your property actually has — an oceanfront terrace and a protected bayside courtyard are different chemistry problems — and we put the specification in writing.

faqs.q: How do king tides and drainage affect outdoor construction here?
faqs.a: Seasonal high tides are a fact of life on low-lying Miami Beach streets, and outdoor construction has to respect them: finished elevations chosen deliberately, drainage that moves water away from the house, and materials at grade that tolerate occasional saltwater without sulking. We design pool decks and terraces with slope, drains, and setdowns planned on paper before demolition. The goal is simple — after a wet October week, your terrace drains and dries while the lawn does the suffering.

outdoor-living.cta_sub: Walk us through the yard and the wish list. We will bring the permit knowledge and a written scope, in English o en español.
